>>>> On the other issues:
>>>>
>>>>    - The news filters have been notoriously finicky from page to page.
>>>>    I've sorted it out now--the "showNews" logic just needed to be tweaked a
>>>>    bit.
>>>>    - In terms of the slow load times, I've been seeing the same thing
>>>>    and this is last on my list to test and optimize after everything else is
>>>>    in place. Part of this will be fixing the placeholders which aren't
>>>>    resolving currently and you're right that production should improve it
>>>>    some.
>>>>    - Forestry page, the spacing and fonts have changed how they work
>>>>    from 1.9:
>>>>       - *v1.9 uses fixed design tokens defined
>>>>       in tailwind.config.js (discrete spacing scale; static text sizes). v4
>>>>       switches to CSS variables and formulas — spacing becomes “any integer
>>>>       × --spacing,” and text sizes/line-heights come from --text-*variables —
>>>>       while prose works the same but plugs into the new variable system.*
>>>>       - For instance, the old system
>>>>          - <div class="mt-8 p-4">
>>>>            <!-- mt-8 = 2rem (32px), p-4 = 1rem (16px) -->
>>>>          - The new system:
>>>>          - <div class="mt-8 p-4">
>>>>            <!-- mt-8 = calc(var(--spacing) * 8)
>>>>                 p-4 = calc(var(--spacing) * 4) -->
>>>>          - I've been working on the base styling and I think I have
>>>>       things restored--there may still be some outliers. I removed the spacing
>>>>       definitions in app.pcss @theme section, which was a carryover from the
>>>>       tailwind.config.js v1.9 but seems to be interfering with the styling we
>>>>       want now.
>>>>    - The accessibility checker issues:
>>>>       - *Four landmark issues*:
>>>>          - navigation--top.vue has the <div class="flex-grow">
>>>>          - navigation-item--secondary.twig has the <span> Activity
>>>>          Calendar </span>
>>>>          - To fix this accessibility issue I added a <nav> as a parent
>>>>          element to main navigation, main navigation items and "utility navigation
>>>>          items" for the secondary nav items which are all labelled now with
>>>>          aria-label
>>>>       - *Modal Accessible Name*:
>>>>          - modal--main.vue had this code and I added an aria-label
>>>>          fallback with a dynamic switch for each modal type and passed the ID down
>>>>          to the component children which should ensure consistency for Screen
>>>>          Readers.
>>>>       - *Role Usage on Nav--Items*: the code referenced is in
>>>>       navigation--items.vue and the problem has to do with the menu role usage.
>>>>       The menu role shouldn't be necessary here since we're using a semantic nav
>>>>       element with a descriptive aria-label so I just removed the roles and this
>>>>       should be clean now.
>>>>
>>>> All that's left on my list now is the performance issues with slow load
>>>> times and placeholder usage.

>>> On the other issues:

>>>    - The news filters have been notoriously finicky from page to page.

>>>    bit.
>>>    - In terms of the slow load times, I've been seeing the same thing
>>>    and this is last on my list to test and optimize after everything else is
>>>    in place. Part of this will be fixing the placeholders which aren't
>>>    resolving currently and you're right that production should improve it
>>>    some.
>>>    - Forestry page, the spacing and fonts have changed how they work
>>>    from 1.9:
>>>       - *v1.9 uses fixed design tokens defined
>>>       in tailwind.config.js (discrete spacing scale; static text sizes). v4
>>>       switches to CSS variables and formulas — spacing becomes “any integer
>>>       × --spacing,” and text sizes/line-heights come from --text-*variables —
>>>       while prose works the same but plugs into the new variable system.*
>>>       - For instance, the old system
>>>          - <div class="mt-8 p-4">
>>>            <!-- mt-8 = 2rem (32px), p-4 = 1rem (16px) -->
>>>          - The new system:
>>>          - <div class="mt-8 p-4">
>>>            <!-- mt-8 = calc(var(--spacing) * 8)
>>>                 p-4 = calc(var(--spacing) * 4) -->
>>>          - I've been working on the base styling and I think I have
>>>       things restored--there may still be some outliers. I removed the spacing
>>>       definitions in app.pcss @theme section, which was a carryover from the
>>>       tailwind.config.js v1.9 but seems to be interfering with the styling we
>>>       want now.
>>>    - The accessibility checker issues:
>>>       - *Four landmark issues*:
>>>          - navigation--top.vue has the <div class="flex-grow">
>>>          - navigation-item--secondary.twig has the <span> Activity
>>>          Calendar </span>
>>>          - To fix this accessibility issue I added a <nav> as a parent
>>>          element to main navigation, main navigation items and "utility navigation
>>>          items" for the secondary nav items which are all labelled now with
>>>          aria-label
>>>       - *Modal Accessible Name*:
>>>          - modal--main.vue had this code and I added an aria-label
>>>          fallback with a dynamic switch for each modal type and passed the ID down
>>>          to the component children which should ensure consistency for Screen
>>>          Readers.
>>>       - *Role Usage on Nav--Items*: the code referenced is in
>>>       navigation--items.vue and the problem has to do with the menu role usage.
>>>       The menu role shouldn't be necessary here since we're using a semantic nav
>>>       element with a descriptive aria-label so I just removed the roles and this
>>>       should be clean now.
>>>
>>> All that's left on my list now is the performance issues with slow load
>>> times and placeholder usage.

> > > > > > • Forestry page, the spacing and fonts have changed how they work from 1.9:
> > > > > >     • v1.9 uses fixed design tokens defined in tailwind.config.js (discrete spacing scale; static text sizes). v4 switches to CSS variables and formulas — spacing becomes “any integer × --spacing,” and text sizes/line-heights come from --text-*variables — while prose works the same but plugs into the new variable system.
> > > > > >     • For instance, the old system
> > > > > >         • <div class="mt-8 p-4">
> > > > > >   <!-- mt-8 = 2rem (32px), p-4 = 1rem (16px) -->
> > > > > >     • The new system:
> > > > > >         • <div class="mt-8 p-4">
> > > > > >   <!-- mt-8 = calc(var(--spacing) * 8)
> > > > > >        p-4 = calc(var(--spacing) * 4) -->
> > > > > >     • I've been working on the base styling and I think I have things restored--there may still be some outliers. I removed the spacing definitions in app.pcss @theme section, which was a carryover from the tailwind.config.js v1.9 but seems to be interfering with the styling we want now.
> > > > > > • The accessibility checker issues:
> > > > > >     • Four landmark issues:
> > > > > >         • navigation--top.vue has the <div class="flex-grow">
> > > > > >         • navigation-item--secondary.twig has the <span> Activity Calendar </span>
> > > > > >         • To fix this accessibility issue I added a <nav> as a parent element to main navigation, main navigation items and "utility navigation items" for the secondary nav items which are all labelled now with aria-label
> > > > > >     • Modal Accessible Name:
> > > > > >         • modal--main.vue had this code and I added an aria-label fallback with a dynamic switch for each modal type and passed the ID down to the component children which should ensure consistency for Screen Readers.
> > > > > >     • Role Usage on Nav--Items: the code referenced is in navigation--items.vue and the problem has to do with the menu role usage. The menu role shouldn't be necessary here since we're using a semantic nav element with a descriptive aria-label so I just removed the roles and this should be clean now.

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 1. Got it. That color is corrected.

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 4. I believe this one was on a checklist from a few months ago so thanks for bringing it up again. The reason for the mismatch is a simple naming convention. The neutral outline color in the old code was outline-gray and in the new code we redefine the color variable rather than swap them out to fit each outline case. This was in part to avoid the repeated use of !important to override variables for particular instances which would occasionally result in unforeseen behavior--making the code a bit cleaner. To fix it, I'll just change the naming convention to "outline-base" to avoid confusion. This is a quick and easy change too if you have a different naming convention you prefer.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 5. Thanks for noting this. Before the update we used focus:outline-* as inline css; however, with the new Tailwind set up we use the outline-* directly and the focus is implied.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 6. Gotcha. Yeah, this was in the aspect-ratio troubleshooting. I reintroduced xl:h-full to the <picture> element and that fixed it.

>>    resolving currently and you're right that production should improve it
>>    some.
>>    - Forestry page, the spacing and fonts have changed how they work
>>    from 1.9:
>>       - *v1.9 uses fixed design tokens defined
>>       in tailwind.config.js (discrete spacing scale; static text sizes). v4
>>       switches to CSS variables and formulas — spacing becomes “any integer
>>       × --spacing,” and text sizes/line-heights come from --text-*variables —
>>       while prose works the same but plugs into the new variable system.*
>>       - For instance, the old system
>>          - <div class="mt-8 p-4">
>>            <!-- mt-8 = 2rem (32px), p-4 = 1rem (16px) -->
>>          - The new system:
>>          - <div class="mt-8 p-4">
>>            <!-- mt-8 = calc(var(--spacing) * 8)
>>                 p-4 = calc(var(--spacing) * 4) -->
>>          - I've been working on the base styling and I think I have
>>       things restored--there may still be some outliers. I removed the spacing
>>       definitions in app.pcss @theme section, which was a carryover from the
>>       tailwind.config.js v1.9 but seems to be interfering with the styling we
>>       want now.
>>    - The accessibility checker issues:
>>       - *Four landmark issues*:
>>          - navigation--top.vue has the <div class="flex-grow">
>>          - navigation-item--secondary.twig has the <span> Activity
>>          Calendar </span>
>>          - To fix this accessibility issue I added a <nav> as a parent
>>          element to main navigation, main navigation items and "utility navigation
>>          items" for the secondary nav items which are all labelled now with
>>          aria-label
>>       - *Modal Accessible Name*:
>>          - modal--main.vue had this code and I added an aria-label
>>          fallback with a dynamic switch for each modal type and passed the ID down
>>          to the component children which should ensure consistency for Screen
>>          Readers.
>>       - *Role Usage on Nav--Items*: the code referenced is in
>>       navigation--items.vue and the problem has to do with the menu role usage.
>>       The menu role shouldn't be necessary here since we're using a semantic nav
>>       element with a descriptive aria-label so I just removed the roles and this
>>       should be clean now.
>>
>> All that's left on my list now is the performance issues with slow load
>> times and placeholder usage.

>>>>>> slightly different from local but this isn't crucial since the database and
>>>>>> assets are going to update to production anyway. So it's safe now to
>>>>>> continue with your points:
>>>>>>
>>>>>>    1. Got it. That color is corrected.
>>>>>>    2. This one has some potential to be meddlesome so I'm working on
>>>>>>    this last--now that is.
>>>>>>    3. This was corrected by removing the stray redactor reference.
>>>>>>    4. I believe this one was on a checklist from a few months ago so
>>>>>>    thanks for bringing it up again. The reason for the mismatch is a simple
>>>>>>    naming convention. The neutral outline color in the old code was
>>>>>>    outline-gray and in the new code we redefine the color variable rather than
>>>>>>    swap them out to fit each outline case. This was in part to avoid the
>>>>>>    repeated use of !important to override variables for particular instances
>>>>>>    which would occasionally result in unforeseen behavior--making the code a
>>>>>>    bit cleaner. To fix it, I'll just change the naming convention to
>>>>>>    "outline-base" to avoid confusion. This is a quick and easy change too if
>>>>>>    you have a different naming convention you prefer.
>>>>>>    5. Thanks for noting this. Before the update we used
>>>>>>    focus:outline-* as inline css; however, with the new Tailwind set up we use
>>>>>>    the outline-* directly and the focus is implied.
>>>>>>    6. Gotcha. Yeah, this was in the aspect-ratio troubleshooting. I
>>>>>>    reintroduced xl:h-full to the <picture> element and that fixed it.
>>>>>>
>>>>>> Other notes:
>>>>>>
>>>>>>    1. I came across one other mismatch with the navigation: the font
>>>>>>    size was a touch smaller so I set it to initial and that has fixed it and I
>>>>>>    see the color is black in dev but gray-600 in production so I set that to
>>>>>>    gray-600.

> > > On the other issues:
> > >
> > > • The news filters have been notoriously finicky from page to page. I've sorted it out now--the "showNews" logic just needed to be tweaked a bit.
> > > • In terms of the slow load times, I've been seeing the same thing and this is last on my list to test and optimize after everything else is in place. Part of this will be fixing the placeholders which aren't resolving currently and you're right that production should improve it some.
> > > • Forestry page, the spacing and fonts have changed how they work from 1.9:
> > >     • v1.9 uses fixed design tokens defined in tailwind.config.js (discrete spacing scale; static text sizes). v4 switches to CSS variables and formulas — spacing becomes “any integer × --spacing,” and text sizes/line-heights come from --text-*variables — while prose works the same but plugs into the new variable system.
> > >     • For instance, the old system
> > >         • <div class="mt-8 p-4">
> > >   <!-- mt-8 = 2rem (32px), p-4 = 1rem (16px) -->
> > >     • The new system:
> > >         • <div class="mt-8 p-4">
> > >   <!-- mt-8 = calc(var(--spacing) * 8)
> > >        p-4 = calc(var(--spacing) * 4) -->
> > >     • I've been working on the base styling and I think I have things restored--there may still be some outliers. I removed the spacing definitions in app.pcss @theme section, which was a carryover from the tailwind.config.js v1.9 but seems to be interfering with the styling we want now.
> > > • The accessibility checker issues:
> > >     • Four landmark issues:
> > >         • navigation--top.vue has the <div class="flex-grow">
> > >         • navigation-item--secondary.twig has the <span> Activity Calendar </span>
> > >         • To fix this accessibility issue I added a <nav> as a parent element to main navigation, main navigation items and "utility navigation items" for the secondary nav items which are all labelled now with aria-label
> > >     • Modal Accessible Name:
> > >         • modal--main.vue had this code and I added an aria-label fallback with a dynamic switch for each modal type and passed the ID down to the component children which should ensure consistency for Screen Readers.
> > >     • Role Usage on Nav--Items: the code referenced is in navigation--items.vue and the problem has to do with the menu role usage. The menu role shouldn't be necessary here since we're using a semantic nav element with a descriptive aria-label so I just removed the roles and this should be clean now.
> > >
> > > All that's left on my list now is the performance issues with slow load times and placeholder usage.

> > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > 1. Got it. That color is corrected.

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > 4. I believe this one was on a checklist from a few months ago so thanks for bringing it up again. The reason for the mismatch is a simple naming convention. The neutral outline color in the old code was outline-gray and in the new code we redefine the color variable rather than swap them out to fit each outline case. This was in part to avoid the repeated use of !important to override variables for particular instances which would occasionally result in unforeseen behavior--making the code a bit cleaner. To fix it, I'll just change the naming convention to "outline-base" to avoid confusion. This is a quick and easy change too if you have a different naming convention you prefer.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > 5. Thanks for noting this. Before the update we used focus:outline-* as inline css; however, with the new Tailwind set up we use the outline-* directly and the focus is implied.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > 6. Gotcha. Yeah, this was in the aspect-ratio troubleshooting. I reintroduced xl:h-full to the <picture> element and that fixed it.

>    - Forestry page, the spacing and fonts have changed how they work from
>    1.9:
>       - *v1.9 uses fixed design tokens defined
>       in tailwind.config.js (discrete spacing scale; static text sizes). v4
>       switches to CSS variables and formulas — spacing becomes “any integer
>       × --spacing,” and text sizes/line-heights come from --text-*variables —
>       while prose works the same but plugs into the new variable system.*
>       - For instance, the old system
>          - <div class="mt-8 p-4">
>            <!-- mt-8 = 2rem (32px), p-4 = 1rem (16px) -->
>          - The new system:
>          - <div class="mt-8 p-4">
>            <!-- mt-8 = calc(var(--spacing) * 8)
>                 p-4 = calc(var(--spacing) * 4) -->
>          - I've been working on the base styling and I think I have
>       things restored--there may still be some outliers. I removed the spacing
>       definitions in app.pcss @theme section, which was a carryover from the
>       tailwind.config.js v1.9 but seems to be interfering with the styling we
>       want now.
>    - The accessibility checker issues:
>       - *Four landmark issues*:
>          - navigation--top.vue has the <div class="flex-grow">
>          - navigation-item--secondary.twig has the <span> Activity
>          Calendar </span>
>          - To fix this accessibility issue I added a <nav> as a parent
>          element to main navigation, main navigation items and "utility navigation
>          items" for the secondary nav items which are all labelled now with
>          aria-label
>       - *Modal Accessible Name*:
>          - modal--main.vue had this code and I added an aria-label
>          fallback with a dynamic switch for each modal type and passed the ID down
>          to the component children which should ensure consistency for Screen
>          Readers.
>       - *Role Usage on Nav--Items*: the code referenced is in
>       navigation--items.vue and the problem has to do with the menu role usage.
>       The menu role shouldn't be necessary here since we're using a semantic nav
>       element with a descriptive aria-label so I just removed the roles and this
>       should be clean now.

>>>>>    3. This was corrected by removing the stray redactor reference.
>>>>>    4. I believe this one was on a checklist from a few months ago so
>>>>>    thanks for bringing it up again. The reason for the mismatch is a simple
>>>>>    naming convention. The neutral outline color in the old code was
>>>>>    outline-gray and in the new code we redefine the color variable rather than
>>>>>    swap them out to fit each outline case. This was in part to avoid the
>>>>>    repeated use of !important to override variables for particular instances
>>>>>    which would occasionally result in unforeseen behavior--making the code a
>>>>>    bit cleaner. To fix it, I'll just change the naming convention to
>>>>>    "outline-base" to avoid confusion. This is a quick and easy change too if
>>>>>    you have a different naming convention you prefer.
>>>>>    5. Thanks for noting this. Before the update we used
>>>>>    focus:outline-* as inline css; however, with the new Tailwind set up we use
>>>>>    the outline-* directly and the focus is implied.
>>>>>    6. Gotcha. Yeah, this was in the aspect-ratio troubleshooting. I
>>>>>    reintroduced xl:h-full to the <picture> element and that fixed it.

On Sep 3, 2025 at 5:32 PM -0600, Eric Phifer <eric@ericphiferllc.com>, wrote:
> On the other issues:
>
> • The news filters have been notoriously finicky from page to page. I've sorted it out now--the "showNews" logic just needed to be tweaked a bit.
> • In terms of the slow load times, I've been seeing the same thing and this is last on my list to test and optimize after everything else is in place. Part of this will be fixing the placeholders which aren't resolving currently and you're right that production should improve it some.
> • Forestry page, the spacing and fonts have changed how they work from 1.9:
>     • v1.9 uses fixed design tokens defined in tailwind.config.js (discrete spacing scale; static text sizes). v4 switches to CSS variables and formulas — spacing becomes “any integer × --spacing,” and text sizes/line-heights come from --text-*variables — while prose works the same but plugs into the new variable system.
>     • For instance, the old system
>         • <div class="mt-8 p-4">
>   <!-- mt-8 = 2rem (32px), p-4 = 1rem (16px) -->
>     • The new system:
>         • <div class="mt-8 p-4">
>   <!-- mt-8 = calc(var(--spacing) * 8)
>        p-4 = calc(var(--spacing) * 4) -->
>     • I've been working on the base styling and I think I have things restored--there may still be some outliers. I removed the spacing definitions in app.pcss @theme section, which was a carryover from the tailwind.config.js v1.9 but seems to be interfering with the styling we want now.
> • The accessibility checker issues:
>     • Four landmark issues:
>         • navigation--top.vue has the <div class="flex-grow">
>         • navigation-item--secondary.twig has the <span> Activity Calendar </span>
>         • To fix this accessibility issue I added a <nav> as a parent element to main navigation, main navigation items and "utility navigation items" for the secondary nav items which are all labelled now with aria-label
>     • Modal Accessible Name:
>         • modal--main.vue had this code and I added an aria-label fallback with a dynamic switch for each modal type and passed the ID down to the component children which should ensure consistency for Screen Readers.
>     • Role Usage on Nav--Items: the code referenced is in navigation--items.vue and the problem has to do with the menu role usage. The menu role shouldn't be necessary here since we're using a semantic nav element with a descriptive aria-label so I just removed the roles and this should be clean now.
>
> All that's left on my list now is the performance issues with slow load times and placeholder usage.

>>>>>> Shaun,
>>>>>>
>>>>>> Regarding Vue2 to Vue3 migration, I figure this one should go in
>>>>>> Project Status.
>>>>>>
>>>>>> *Do we have any other options to prevent the close of the menus after
>>>>>> this code finishes?*: There are always other options, like your
>>>>>> loading modal solution; however, if our primary goal is accessibility and
>>>>>> usability then the loading modal will increase a user pain-point, i.e.
>>>>>> increased time to wait before they can access the information on the page.
>>>>>> So the question I would ask is: what will give users the fastest, most
>>>>>> consistent experience?
>>>>>>
>>>>>> I'll reference some other ideas later on.
>>>>>>
>>>>>> *Why does it work better in Production?*: "Dev mode" in Servd might
>>>>>> be a factor, which introduces additional operations that don't run in
>>>>>> Production. There are also configurations enabled specific to development
>>>>>> that Mark setup, which is normal.
>>>>>>
>>>>>> I ran Lighthouse on the dev environment and production pages for
>>>>>> "Adult Hockey", these were the results (dev on left | production on right):
>>>>>> <Screenshot 2024-05-16 at 12-09-12 Lighthouse Report Viewer.png>
>>>>>>  <Screenshot 2024-05-16 at 12-11-55 Lighthouse Report Viewer.png>
>>>>>> This test at least doesn't show much difference in performance and if
>>>>>> I refresh in production and hover over a menu to open the dropdown the soft
>>>>>> refresh does still occur and resets the dropdown. It does seem to happen
>>>>>> faster in production so I see what you mean there, but this is likely just
>>>>>> because there's nothing to get. In other words, it immediately returns
>>>>>> false and has no further payload to return.
>>>>>>
>>>>>> Breaking down the operation...
>>>>>>  1. The page loads all initial page elements
>>>>>>  2. Loading... is the default div element
>>>>>>  • the code checks CraftCMS if there is a closure to display via
>>>>>> GraphQL query
>>>>>>  3. The closure element (if true) or an empty div (if false) is
>>>>>> injected into the DOM tree, which causes the soft reload.
>>>>>> I have checked a couple of possibilities today:
>>>>>>  • v-show instead of v-if because v-show is present in the DOM before
>>>>>> and after and so shouldn't have the soft refresh; however, upon testing it
>>>>>> there is no change to the issue.
>>>>>>  • I reviewed the getters, store, mutations and actions JS files -
>>>>>> these manage load states of various components; however, I have not found
>>>>>> anything to be improved or optimized for this use case.
>>>>>> [ Side note: I discovered a file called lazy-load-component which I
>>>>>> attempted to use to fix the modal problem, but no success. ]
>>>>>>
>>>>>> Answering the question "is it necessary?": Vue has an article that
>>>>>> helps this question <https://v2.vuejs.org/lts/>. They say to ask 3
>>>>>> questions:
>>>>>>  1. Is the website stable and working well?
>>>>>>  2. Does the website expect continued new feature development into
>>>>>> the future?
>>>>>>  3. Is there a pain-point or bottleneck that can only be solved by
>>>>>> upgrading?
>>>>>> You would be able to answer the first two better, but I can at least
>>>>>> speak to the third: accessibility is likely that pain-point / bottleneck.
>>>>>> The further I dig into this the more I'm finding conflicting advice on how
>>>>>> to utilize Vue, even for Vue 2, which seems to stem from two reasons:
>>>>>>  1.  Vue 2.7 included several concepts from Vue 3 and so some of the
>>>>>> documentation and blogs use 2.7 syntax and simply say Vue2. Aspen is using
>>>>>> v2.5.17 and so doesn't have access to several features, which I'll go into
>>>>>> later.
>>>>>>  2. EOL occurred in December of last year, but it's been
>>>>>> transitioning out since 2020. This problem is compounded with plugins
>>>>>> related to Vue. @storybook plugin for instance doesn't even have code for
>>>>>> any Vue2 version anymore - I'll reference this again later.
>>>>>> Could we kick the can down the road? We could; however, in Vue2 the
>>>>>> website "will no longer receive updates, including security and
>>>>>> browser compatibility fixes", which is something I've noted
>>>>>> while working on accessibility - e.g. different accessibility experiences
>>>>>> on Safari, Firefox and Chromium based browsers.
>>>>>>
>>>>>> The dependencies associated with Vue will no longer be supported as
>>>>>> well and some have entirely removed their packages already, like this:
>>>>>> <Screenshot 2024-05-16 at 10.46.23 AM.png>
>>>>>> <Screenshot 2024-05-16 at 10.43.23 AM.png>
>>>>>> I actually can't find any Aspen code that utilizes the storybook
>>>>>> plugin so I don't see any reason for it to be here, but it's one of several
>>>>>> examples where Vue2 support is fading.
>>>>>>
>>>>>> Because of this Vue recommends building your own in-house Vue2
>>>>>> compatible plugins and supporting them yourself. This will take
>>>>>> considerably more man power and time than I think Aspen wants to put into
>>>>>> it. So in the long run upgrading will cost Aspen less time and money.
>>>>>>
>>>>>> Could we get the modal and loading to work without upgrading?
>>>>>> Probably, *but* there are built-in parts of Vue3 that specifically
>>>>>> enhance and simplify modals and loading. For instance:
>>>>>>  • Vue3 introduced <Teleport>
>>>>>> <https://vuejs.org/guide/built-ins/teleport.html>: a reliable way to
>>>>>> handle modals
>>>>>>  • A large portion of the Aspen code relies on "types" - Vue3 is
>>>>>> entirely Typescript and better supports this methodology.
>>>>>>  • Composition API
>>>>>> <https://vuejs.org/guide/extras/composition-api-faq.html> (CAPI) -
>>>>>> this is the single largest advantage to Vue3 for the modals & loading
>>>>>> because it supports Reactivity APIs and Lifecycle Hooks - things like ref()
>>>>>> and onMounted(), which we are using older versions of utilizing mixins and
>>>>>> the Options API. CAPI, however, solves all the drawbacks of mixins
>>>>>> <https://vuejs.org/guide/reusability/composables#vs-mixins>, the
>>>>>> primary logic reuse mechanism for Options API - which is what Mark
>>>>>> primarily implemented throughout.To say it another way, I don't
>>>>>> have a Vue2 solution to these two pressing problems yet, but I do have Vue3
>>>>>> solutions for them. Being able to utilize these features will shorten the
>>>>>> time needed to fix accessibility and future issues.
>>>>>>
>>>>>> What exactly will the migration entail? I discovered that Vue has a
>>>>>> package called @vue/compat
>>>>>> <https://v3-migration.vuejs.org/migration-build> which essentially
>>>>>> is a transition between Vue2 and 3 which allows functionality to continue
>>>>>> with Vue2 syntax while sorting out the error and warning messages that
>>>>>> bring the code up to Vue3 syntax compliance. Using this, I think we can
>>>>>> significantly reduce the time to production for Vue3.
>>>>>>
>>>>>> These are the three basic parts to the migration:
>>>>>>  1. *Check Compatibility*: Use the Vue 3 compatibility build to
>>>>>> identify any issues with the current setup.
>>>>>>  2. *Upgrade and Test*: Upgrade dependencies and test each one
>>>>>> incrementally to identify breaking changes.
>>>>>>  3. *Seek Alternatives*: If a package is not compatible with Vue 3,
>>>>>> look for actively maintained alternatives.
>>>>>> Updating the packages and dependencies is essential to the migration,
>>>>>> this is a quick overview:
>>>>>>
>>>>>> *Direct Vue 2 Dependencies* 1. *vue*: update to vue@next for Vue 3.
>>>>>>  2. *vue-template-compiler*: Replace this with @vue/compiler-sfc in
>>>>>> Vue 3.
>>>>>> *Vue Ecosystem Packages* 1. *vue-loader*: Ensure use of the version
>>>>>> compatible with Vue 3, which would be vue-loader@next.
>>>>>>  2. *eslint-plugin-vue*: Update to a version that supports Vue 3.
>>>>>>  3. *@storybook/vue*: Update to use the version compatible with Vue
>>>>>> 3 or remove.
>>>>>> *Vue Plugins and Libraries* 1. *vue-clickaway*: Check if there's a
>>>>>> version compatible with Vue 3 or find an alternative.
>>>>>>  2. *vue-gallery-slideshow*: Verify compatibility or look for an
>>>>>> alternative library.
>>>>>>  3. *vue-wait*: Check for Vue 3 support or find an alternative.
>>>>>>  4. *vuex*: Upgrade to Vuex 4, which is designed for Vue 3.
>>>>>>  5. *vuex-persistedstate*: Check for a compatible version.
>>>>>>  6. *vuex-shared-mutations*: Verify if it's compatible with Vue 3 or
>>>>>> find an alternative.
>>>>>> *Other Dependencies to Review* 1. *@storybook/addon-essentials,
>>>>>> @storybook/addons, @storybook/builder-webpack5, @storybook/core,
>>>>>> @storybook/core-common*: Update to Vue 3 compatible versions or
>>>>>> remove.
>>>>>>  2. *babel-loader*: Should work as is, but make sure it's compatible
>>>>>> with other dependencies.
>>>>>>  3. *css-loader, style-loader*: Generally should work, but ensure
>>>>>> compatibility with Vue 3 setup.
>>>>>>  4. *ts-loader, typescript*: Ensure they are configured correctly
>>>>>> for Vue 3 and TypeScript.
>>>>>>  5. *tailwindcss and related plugins*: Check compatibility but they
>>>>>> are generally framework-agnostic.
>>>>>>  6. *axios, core-js, moment, moment-timezone*: These should work as
>>>>>> they are not directly tied to Vue.
>>>>>>  7. *node*: Update to v20 so that Vuex will work.
>>>>>> *Be aware*: Vue3 does not support IE11 at all; however, Microsoft
>>>>>> has said they have stopped supporting IE as well
>>>>>> <https://blogs.windows.com/windowsexperience/2022/06/15/internet-explorer-11-has-retired-and-is-officially-out-of-support-what-you-need-to-know/>.
>>>>>> So I think this is fairly standard now - just a heads up.
>>>>>>
>>>>>> *Bonus*: there is a possible bonus to Vue3 which is usage of Vite
>>>>>> <https://vitejs.dev>, which could simplify our local dev environment
>>>>>> issue and its sole purpose is to speed up front-end operations. It works
>>>>>> very well in the vue-project I built, but of course that doesn't have
>>>>>> CraftCMS, Docker or a database utilized so there will be some variances in
>>>>>> setup, but the results should be the same.
>>>>>>
>>>>>> *Final Thoughts*in the long run, the time and money saved for Aspen
>>>>>> from upgrading I think will be worth the extra time and work now.
>>>>>>
>>>>>> In summary, Vue3 will take less time to maintain, has actively
>>>>>> maintained package options, which means less bugs, and is actively
>>>>>> supported by the Vue community, which means easier to find solutions when
>>>>>> bugs arise - like the ones we're running into for accessibility.
>>>>>>
>>>>>> I've tried to be as thorough as possible but let me know if you have
>>>>>> any questions.
>>>>>>
>>>>>> Thanks for your help and diligence.
>>>>>>

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Do we have any other options to prevent the close of the menus after this code finishes?: There are always other options, like your loading modal solution; however, if our primary goal is accessibility and usability then the loading modal will increase a user pain-point, i.e. increased time to wait before they can access the information on the page. So the question I would ask is: what will give users the fastest, most consistent experience?

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > I'll reference some other ideas later on.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Why does it work better in Production?: "Dev mode" in Servd might be a factor, which introduces additional operations that don't run in Production. There are also configurations enabled specific to development that Mark setup, which is normal.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > I ran Lighthouse on the dev environment and production pages for "Adult Hockey", these were the results (dev on left | production on right):

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > This test at least doesn't show much difference in performance and if I refresh in production and hover over a menu to open the dropdown the soft refresh does still occur and resets the dropdown. It does seem to happen faster in production so I see what you mean there, but this is likely just because there's nothing to get. In other words, it immediately returns false and has no further payload to return.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Breaking down the operation...
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >  1. The page loads all initial page elements
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >  2. Loading... is the default div element
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >  • the code checks CraftCMS if there is a closure to display via GraphQL query
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >  3. The closure element (if true) or an empty div (if false) is injected into the DOM tree, which causes the soft reload.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > I have checked a couple of possibilities today:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >  • v-show instead of v-if because v-show is present in the DOM before and after and so shouldn't have the soft refresh; however, upon testing it there is no change to the issue.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >  • I reviewed the getters, store, mutations and actions JS files - these manage load states of various components; however, I have not found anything to be improved or optimized for this use case.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > [ Side note: I discovered a file called lazy-load-component which I attempted to use to fix the modal problem, but no success. ]
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Answering the question "is it necessary?": Vue has an article that helps this question. They say to ask 3 questions:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >  1. Is the website stable and working well?
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >  2. Does the website expect continued new feature development into the future?
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >  3. Is there a pain-point or bottleneck that can only be solved by upgrading?
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > You would be able to answer the first two better, but I can at least speak to the third: accessibility is likely that pain-point / bottleneck. The further I dig into this the more I'm finding conflicting advice on how to utilize Vue, even for Vue 2, which seems to stem from two reasons:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >  1.  Vue 2.7 included several concepts from Vue 3 and so some of the documentation and blogs use 2.7 syntax and simply say Vue2. Aspen is using v2.5.17 and so doesn't have access to several features, which I'll go into later.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >  2. EOL occurred in December of last year, but it's been transitioning out since 2020. This problem is compounded with plugins related to Vue. @storybook plugin for instance doesn't even have code for any Vue2 version anymore - I'll reference this again later.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Could we kick the can down the road? We could; however, in Vue2 the website "will no longer receive updates, including security and browser compatibility fixes", which is something I've noted while working on accessibility - e.g. different accessibility experiences on Safari, Firefox and Chromium based browsers.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > The dependencies associated with Vue will no longer be supported as well and some have entirely removed their packages already, like this:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > <Screenshot 2024-05-16 at 10.46.23 AM.png>
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > <Screenshot 2024-05-16 at 10.43.23 AM.png>
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > I actually can't find any Aspen code that utilizes the storybook plugin so I don't see any reason for it to be here, but it's one of several examples where Vue2 support is fading.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Because of this Vue recommends building your own in-house Vue2 compatible plugins and supporting them yourself. This will take considerably more man power and time than I think Aspen wants to put into it. So in the long run upgrading will cost Aspen less time and money.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Could we get the modal and loading to work without upgrading? Probably, but there are built-in parts of Vue3 that specifically enhance and simplify modals and loading. For instance:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >  • Vue3 introduced <Teleport>: a reliable way to handle modals
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >  • A large portion of the Aspen code relies on "types" - Vue3 is entirely Typescript and better supports this methodology.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >  • Composition API (CAPI) - this is the single largest advantage to Vue3 for the modals & loading because it supports Reactivity APIs and Lifecycle Hooks - things like ref() and onMounted(), which we are using older versions of utilizing mixins and the Options API. CAPI, however, solves all the drawbacks of mixins, the primary logic reuse mechanism for Options API - which is what Mark primarily implemented throughout.To say it another way, I don't have a Vue2 solution to these two pressing problems yet, but I do have Vue3 solutions for them. Being able to utilize these features will shorten the time needed to fix accessibility and future issues.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > What exactly will the migration entail? I discovered that Vue has a package called @vue/compat which essentially is a transition between Vue2 and 3 which allows functionality to continue with Vue2 syntax while sorting out the error and warning messages that bring the code up to Vue3 syntax compliance. Using this, I think we can significantly reduce the time to production for Vue3.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > These are the three basic parts to the migration:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >  1. Check Compatibility: Use the Vue 3 compatibility build to identify any issues with the current setup.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >  2. Upgrade and Test: Upgrade dependencies and test each one incrementally to identify breaking changes.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >  3. Seek Alternatives: If a package is not compatible with Vue 3, look for actively maintained alternatives.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Updating the packages and dependencies is essential to the migration, this is a quick overview:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Direct Vue 2 Dependencies 1. vue: update to vue@next for Vue 3.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >  2. vue-template-compiler: Replace this with @vue/compiler-sfc in Vue 3.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Vue Ecosystem Packages 1. vue-loader: Ensure use of the version compatible with Vue 3, which would be vue-loader@next.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >  2. eslint-plugin-vue: Update to a version that supports Vue 3.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >  3. @storybook/vue: Update to use the version compatible with Vue 3 or remove.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Vue Plugins and Libraries 1. vue-clickaway: Check if there's a version compatible with Vue 3 or find an alternative.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >  2. vue-gallery-slideshow: Verify compatibility or look for an alternative library.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >  3. vue-wait: Check for Vue 3 support or find an alternative.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >  4. vuex: Upgrade to Vuex 4, which is designed for Vue 3.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >  5. vuex-persistedstate: Check for a compatible version.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >  6. vuex-shared-mutations: Verify if it's compatible with Vue 3 or find an alternative.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Other Dependencies to Review 1. @storybook/addon-essentials, @storybook/addons, @storybook/builder-webpack5, @storybook/core, @storybook/core-common: Update to Vue 3 compatible versions or remove.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >  2. babel-loader: Should work as is, but make sure it's compatible with other dependencies.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >  3. css-loader, style-loader: Generally should work, but ensure compatibility with Vue 3 setup.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >  4. ts-loader, typescript: Ensure they are configured correctly for Vue 3 and TypeScript.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >  5. tailwindcss and related plugins: Check compatibility but they are generally framework-agnostic.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >  6. axios, core-js, moment, moment-timezone: These should work as they are not directly tied to Vue.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >  7. node: Update to v20 so that Vuex will work.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Be aware: Vue3 does not support IE11 at all; however, Microsoft has said they have stopped supporting IE as well. So I think this is fairly standard now - just a heads up.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Bonus: there is a possible bonus to Vue3 which is usage of Vite, which could simplify our local dev environment issue and its sole purpose is to speed up front-end operations. It works very well in the vue-project I built, but of course that doesn't have CraftCMS, Docker or a database utilized so there will be some variances in setup, but the results should be the same.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Final Thoughtsin the long run, the time and money saved for Aspen from upgrading I think will be worth the extra time and work now.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > In summary, Vue3 will take less time to maintain, has actively maintained package options, which means less bugs, and is actively supported by the Vue community, which means easier to find solutions when bugs arise - like the ones we're running into for accessibility.
